unchanged_frozen_unit.section: A B S T R A C T
unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: This paper describes a comprehensive analysis of a hybrid energy system (HES) when satisfying the load demand of an off-grid, rural and hilly community in Bangladesh. Different combinations of HES, such as PV/Pump-hydro storage (PHS), Diesel/PHS, and PV/Diesel/Battery, are formulated, analysed, and compared using hybrid opti­ mization of multiple energy resources (HOMER) software. The system configurations, together with the size and selection of system components, are suitably modelled and optimised with the least cost of energy (COE), net present cost (NPC), and $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions. In addition, to illustrate the adaptability and the economic benefits of the studied systems, the scalability of the system is evaluated by changing the load demand and the size of the generator. The study is further extended to include a sensitivity analysis on the uncertain parameters in connection with the climatic data and hardware components. Results indicate that the cost of energy for a pumped HES with a single diesel generator is higher $(0.27\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ than that with two small generators (0.24 $\$/\mathrm{kWh}$ . The energy cost for the optimised PV/Diesel/PHS system $(0.27\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ is found to be significantly lower than those of both PV/PHS (0.43\$/kWh) and Diesel/PHS $(0.41\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ options. This research identifies that the PV/Diesel/PHS system is more cost-effective than the PV/Diesel/Battery-based hybrid system, with cost of en­ ergy at $0.34\$/k W h$ . Results indicate that the genetic algorithm (GA) method provides cost effective and sus­ tainable solution than the HOMER software tool.

source_spans.text: This paper describes a comprehensive analysis of a hybrid energy system (HES) when satisfying the load demand of an off-grid, rural and hilly community in Bangladesh.

Different combinations of HES, such as PV/Pump-hydro storage (PHS), Diesel/PHS, and PV/Diesel/Battery, are formulated, analysed, and compared using hybrid opti­ mization of multiple energy resources (HOMER) software.

The system configurations, together with the size and selection of system components, are suitably modelled and optimised with the least cost of energy (COE), net present cost (NPC), and $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions.
In addition, to illustrate the adaptability and the economic benefits of the studied systems, the scalability of the system is evaluated by changing the load demand and the size of the generator.
The study is further extended to include a sensitivity analysis on the uncertain parameters in connection with the climatic data and hardware components.
Results indicate that the cost of energy for a pumped HES with a single diesel generator is higher $(0.27\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ than that with two small generators (0.24 $\$/\mathrm{kWh}$ .

The energy cost for the optimised PV/Diesel/PHS system $(0.27\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ is found to be significantly lower than those of both PV/PHS (0.43\$/kWh) and Diesel/PHS $(0.41\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ options.
This research identifies that the PV/Diesel/PHS system is more cost-effective than the PV/Diesel/Battery-based hybrid system, with cost of en­ ergy at $0.34\$/k W h$ .
Results indicate that the genetic algorithm (GA) method provides cost effective and sus­ tainable solution than the HOMER software tool.

Unfortunately, the rural communities, especially in the hilly areas, still have no or little electricity access in Bangladesh when they have the same rights and deserve the same level of respect as the urban communities.
To meet this growing electricity demand, the reserves of coal and natural gas are being exhausted at an alarming rate in Bangladesh [4].

In the global perspective, a major transition to the sustainable energy solutions is already underway due mainly to a gradual decline in the availability of conventional energy reserves, the need to ensure a reliable and sus­ tainable energy supply, and the predicted uncertainty in the energy prices resulting from the unpredictable disparity between demand and supply, and the global climate change target to cut the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions by

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: $50{-}80\%$ by 2050 [5]. These national and international energy exi­ gencies have prompted a search for optimal and renewable energy (RE) solutions to satisfy the increased load requirements in Bangladesh [6]. Although the development of Bangladesh’s power sector in recent years has been remarkable (covering $90\%$ with the grid electricity), its per capita electricity consumption is still significantly lower (382kWh/ capita) than the world’s average (3127 kWh/capita) as well as those of South Asian countries [7]. In addition, the effective implementation and configuration of the RE technologies is still far way off the commercial dimension in Bangladesh [8]. Since the country’s economy is in transi­ tion from the low-level to middle-level income and since the energy consumption and economic development is closely interrelated, the current pace of electricity production is inadequate to satisfy its rising demand [1]. Moreover, the significant share of electricity generated by either natural gas or imported furnace oil or coal contributes to the environmental damage. In this context, environmental emissions can be significantly decreased by reducing the dependency on the conventional fuels and applying innovative RE technologies [9–11]. However, RE resources alone in off-grid areas are currently incapable of providing uninterrupted energy supply due to their unpredictable availability and heavy reliance on the environmental conditions [12–14]. Thus, HESs have been the research focus in recent years. For example, integrating the combustion-based engines or large banks of batteries with the solar PV-based RE systems have already been reported to be financially attractive [6,15,16]. While a short literature review in relation to this research is presented in Section 2 of this paper, it is apparent that the PV/Diesel/PHS-based hybrid system for the mountainous areas in Bangladesh has not been investigated or studied yet. Thus, the key ob­ jectives of this paper include:

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Because of the availability, easy installation, high energy and power density, and high efficiency, the electrochemical storage systems are extensively used in the stand-alone HESs, as presented in Table 1. However, their limited lifetimes and the requirement of frequent maintenance are problematic, particularly for areas where access to the mainland is difficult [17,18]. In addition, the disposal of the chemical storage systems poses a practical difficulty in the mountainous areas. Therefore, the mechanical storage systems, such as a pump-hydro op­ tion, could be an alternative to the battery storage systems in the remote areas if a water supply is available. The use of pump-hydro storage in stand-alone power generation facility has recently been emerged to improve the overall sustainability of the low-carbon energy system [19–22]. Its key benefits include a shorter payback period, faster response to the load demand, longer lifetime, and lower maintenance cost than the other systems [23,24].

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: While methods vary from study to study, most of the analyses pre­ sented in Table 2 are clean-energy-based HESs. The study of sizing optimisation is paramount before installing a HES, and it plays a sig­ nificant role in making capital investment decision. In this regard, Kanzumba Kusakana [39] carried out a feasibility study on an off-grid hydrokinetic system configuration with pump-hydro storage for the application in a remote area and found that it was more economic (COE $=0.248\Phi/\mathrm{kWh})$ than a comparable battery storage option $(\mathrm{COE}=0.291\$ $\$1\mathrm{kWh}$ for providing a reliable power supply to the households in the selected zone. However, the author did not examine the load scalability and the uncertainties associated with the meteorological data. Ma et al. [18] optimised a PV/PHS-based power generation scheme for a remote and stand-alone community using a genetic algorithm (GA) and reported that it was economically feasible $\displaystyle{(\mathrm{COE}=0.289\S/\mathrm{kWh})}$ for reliably satisfying the electricity demand. In another study, Ma et al. [40] determined that a PV/Wind/PHS system has more economic benefits than a PV/Wind/Battery system. Unlike these studies, the present study investigates the integration of supplementary prime movers, uncertainty associated with the meteorological data, and the degradation of the hardware systems (PV, and converter). Rathore and Patidar [19] ana­ lysed a PV/Wind/PHS-based stand-alone microgrid system for an offgrid community and reported that a PHS-based system was both economically and environmentally better than a battery-based storage configuration. Another PV/PHS system was examined using a GA with various PV tracking technologies by Shabani and Mahmoudimehr [24] and the results were compared with those for a PV/Battery option. The findings from their study indicated that the latter had a $76\%$ higher COE than the former. Ayodele et al. [41] optimally selected a PHS-based PV/ Wind energy system for a stand-alone community using a binary sortand-search algorithm. They found that a PV/Wind/PHS system had the lowest COE out of all the different configurations studied. A gridintegrated PV/PHS system was studied by Li et al. [42] and they showed that variable renewable energy had significant effects on the balance of a grid’s supply and demand. They investigated this aspect by absorbing the surplus PV power by pump-hydro storage system, which greatly reduced the power output from the studied medium-scale power generation units. It is evident from these analyses that the hybrid sys­ tems supplemented by the diesel generators were not adequately studied and the detailed sensitivity analysis of such systems is scarce in the literature.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: While methods vary from study to study, most of the analyses pre­ sented in Table 2 are clean-energy-based HESs. The study of sizing optimisation is paramount before installing a HES, and it plays a sig­ nificant role in making capital investment decision. In this regard, Kanzumba Kusakana [39] carried out a feasibility study on an off-grid hydrokinetic system configuration with pump-hydro storage for the application in a remote area and found that it was more economic (COE $=0.248\Phi/\mathrm{kWh})$ than a comparable battery storage option $(\mathrm{COE}=0.291\$ $\$1\mathrm{kWh}$ for providing a reliable power supply to the households in the selected zone. However, the author did not examine the load scalability and the uncertainties associated with the meteorological data. Ma et al. [18] optimised a PV/PHS-based power generation scheme for a remote and stand-alone community using a genetic algorithm (GA) and reported that it was economically feasible $\displaystyle{(\mathrm{COE}=0.289\S/\mathrm{kWh})}$ for reliably satisfying the electricity demand. In another study, Ma et al. [40] determined that a PV/Wind/PHS system has more economic benefits than a PV/Wind/Battery system. Unlike these studies, the present study investigates the integration of supplementary prime movers, uncertainty associated with the meteorological data, and the degradation of the hardware systems (PV, and converter). Rathore and Patidar [19] ana­ lysed a PV/Wind/PHS-based stand-alone microgrid system for an offgrid community and reported that a PHS-based system was both economically and environmentally better than a battery-based storage configuration. Another PV/PHS system was examined using a GA with various PV tracking technologies by Shabani and Mahmoudimehr [24] and the results were compared with those for a PV/Battery option. The findings from their study indicated that the latter had a $76\%$ higher COE than the former. Ayodele et al. [41] optimally selected a PHS-based PV/ Wind energy system for a stand-alone community using a binary sortand-search algorithm. They found that a PV/Wind/PHS system had the lowest COE out of all the different configurations studied. A gridintegrated PV/PHS system was studied by Li et al. [42] and they showed that variable renewable energy had significant effects on the balance of a grid’s supply and demand. They investigated this aspect by absorbing the surplus PV power by pump-hydro storage system, which greatly reduced the power output from the studied medium-scale power generation units. It is evident from these analyses that the hybrid sys­ tems supplemented by the diesel generators were not adequately studied and the detailed sensitivity analysis of such systems is scarce in the literature.

The study of sizing optimisation is paramount before installing a HES, and it plays a sig­ nificant role in making capital investment decision.

In this regard, Kanzumba Kusakana [39] carried out a feasibility study on an off-grid hydrokinetic system configuration with pump-hydro storage for the application in a remote area and found that it was more economic (COE $=0.248\Phi/\mathrm{kWh})$ than a comparable battery storage option $(\mathrm{COE}=0.291\$ $\$1\mathrm{kWh}$ for providing a reliable power supply to the households in the selected zone.
However, the author did not examine the load scalability and the uncertainties associated with the meteorological data.

Ma et al. [18] optimised a PV/PHS-based power generation scheme for a remote and stand-alone community using a genetic algorithm (GA) and reported that it was economically feasible $\displaystyle{(\mathrm{COE}=0.289\S/\mathrm{kWh})}$ for reliably satisfying the electricity demand.
In another study, Ma et al. [40] determined that a PV/Wind/PHS system has more economic benefits than a PV/Wind/Battery system.

Unlike these studies, the present study investigates the integration of supplementary prime movers, uncertainty associated with the meteorological data, and the degradation of the hardware systems (PV, and converter).

Rathore and Patidar [19] ana­ lysed a PV/Wind/PHS-based stand-alone microgrid system for an offgrid community and reported that a PHS-based system was both economically and environmentally better than a battery-based storage configuration.
Another PV/PHS system was examined using a GA with various PV tracking technologies by Shabani and Mahmoudimehr [24] and the results were compared with those for a PV/Battery option.
The findings from their study indicated that the latter had a $76\%$ higher COE than the former.
Ayodele et al. [41] optimally selected a PHS-based PV/ Wind energy system for a stand-alone community using a binary sortand-search algorithm.
They found that a PV/Wind/PHS system had the lowest COE out of all the different configurations studied.
A gridintegrated PV/PHS system was studied by Li et al. [42] and they showed that variable renewable energy had significant effects on the balance of a grid’s supply and demand.
They investigated this aspect by absorbing the surplus PV power by pump-hydro storage system, which greatly reduced the power output from the studied medium-scale power generation units.

It is evident from these analyses that the hybrid sys­ tems supplemented by the diesel generators were not adequately studied and the detailed sensitivity analysis of such systems is scarce in the literature.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: A few studies have been reported on the PV/Diesel/PHS system. In this context, Awan et al. [28] carried out a techno-economic perfor­ mance analysis to assess the feasibility of stand-alone application of a PV/Diesel/PHS system in Saudi Arabia. They found that the system had a COE of $0.19\Phi/\mathrm{kWh}$ with a renewable fraction of only $27\%$ . Although they investigated PV/Diesel/PHS one, the load scalability, the uncer­ tainty analysis, and the degradation of the hardware components were not included in their study. In another study, an optimised hybrid PV/ Diesel/PHS option was carried out by Makhdoomi and Askarzadeh [43] using modified crow search algorithm. However, a comparative analysis between PHS and battery storage along the detailed sensitivity analysis was not reported in their analysis.

Das et al. [48] studied and proposed a PV/Micro-hydro/Diesel/Battery system for an off-shore area in Bangladesh. They reported that the proposed system exhibited a COE of $0.206\$4$ which was $28\%$ cheaper than the diesel generator. Nurunnabi et al. [49] carried out a feasibility analysis of an off- and ongrid PV/Wind-based HES at different areas in Bangladesh, including the studied area considered in this study (Sitakunda). Results of their analysis indicated that the COE of PV/Wind option for off- and on-grid are $0.477\mathbb{\mathbb{S}}/\mathrm{kWh}$ and $0.064\Phi/\mathrm{kWh}$ , respectively. However, they did not consider the PHS-based storage technology and RE was not sup­ plemented by the diesel generator. The present study goes further by examining a detailed comparative analysis between a PHS and a batterybased option.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: Studies on different HESs in different regions of Bangladesh have been focused on PV/Diesel/Battery [44], PV/Wind/Battery [45], PV/ Wind/Diesel/Battery [8,46], PV/Wind/Diesel/Biogas [6], and PV/ Biomass/Diesel/Battery [47] configurations. Das et al. [48] studied and proposed a PV/Micro-hydro/Diesel/Battery system for an off-shore area in Bangladesh. They reported that the proposed system exhibited a COE of $0.206\$4$ which was $28\%$ cheaper than the diesel generator. Nurunnabi et al. [49] carried out a feasibility analysis of an off- and ongrid PV/Wind-based HES at different areas in Bangladesh, including the studied area considered in this study (Sitakunda). Results of their analysis indicated that the COE of PV/Wind option for off- and on-grid are $0.477\mathbb{\mathbb{S}}/\mathrm{kWh}$ and $0.064\Phi/\mathrm{kWh}$ , respectively. However, they did not consider the PHS-based storage technology and RE was not sup­ plemented by the diesel generator. The present study goes further by examining a detailed comparative analysis between a PHS and a batterybased option.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Eltamaly et al. [50] carried out a load management strategy to determine the optimal size of the PV/Wind/Diesel/FC/Battery-based HES using PSO technique and compared with the HOMER. They considered two different types of load demand on priority basis such as high and low. They found that the COE was comparable between PSO algorithm (0.2805\$/kWh) and HOMER (0.2774\$/kWh) when both loads were considered. However, they varied only the low priority load demand and did not consider the scalability of load demand i.e. increasing or decreasing the total load requirements. A hybrid PV/ Wind/Battery was optimised using GA-PSO by Ghorbani et al. [51] and compared with the HOMER. The authors reported that the GA-PSO had slightly lower, yet comparable COE (0.508\$/kWh) than that of the HOMER $(0.51\$14)$ . In another study, Fodhil et al. [52] also found that the PSO offers lower cost (0.38\$/kWh) than the HOMER (0.40 $\$1\mathrm{kWh}$ in optimising the HES. In this study, HOMER tool is used because of its simplicity [53] and quick searching ability [54] to find the optimal sizing of the hardware components. Although the current study uses the standard HOMER tool, the analysis goes beyond the standard application of HOMER by thoroughly examining the objective functions, the various uncertainties, and the different consequential performance indicators.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: A schematic layout of the PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro storage system designed to satisfy the load demand $(\mathrm{P_{L}})$ of a small remote community consisting of 50 households is presented in Fig. 1. A direct current (DC) load bus is linked to the PV panel while the alternative current (AC) bus is connected with both diesel generator and the pump-hydro storage system. The DC power generated by the PV module $(\mathrm{P_{PV}})$ is converted to AC power $(\mathrm{{P}_{\mathrm{{inv}}}})$ through an inverter. The excess energy (EE) produced by the PV module after the load demand is satisfied is used to power the pump $(\mathrm{P_{P}})$ to either lift water $\left(\mathsf{Q}_{\mathsf{w}}\right)$ to the upper reservoir or drain down to the lower basin $(\mathrm{\bfP_{EE}})$ when the reservoir reaches its maximum level. The turbine is used to supply power $(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{T}})$ when the production of PV power is not sufficient to meet the electricity demand and the load is under the specified load ratio of the diesel generator ( $30\%$ of its rated power).

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: A well-structured framework is necessary to optimise a HES that can consistently satisfy the load requirements for a stand-alone remote area. The optimisation framework representing this current study is shown in Fig. 2. The HOMER software operates in three different phases. In the first phase, a conceptual system architecture (Fig. 1) is developed based on existing renewable energy and meteorological data. In this phase, the electric power requirement of the selected site is also assessed (Table 3 and presented in Fig. 5) and introduced in the HOMER optimisation tool along with the technical characteristics and economic data of different components (Table 4). In the second phase, an investigation delivers a group of hybrid system options showing the minimisation of NPC and COE under specified constraints. In the third phase, the different system configurations are compared in terms of their technical, economic, and environmental parameters in order to select the optimal hybrid option. In summary, the simulation uses energy balance of HES components with the given constraints, load profile, and meteorological data to calculate the costs. HOMER then displays a list of configurations, sorted by net present cost. In this process, the best solution is selected from among all scenarios depending on the selected criterion (e.g. minimi­ zation of net present costs). In this process, HOMER does not provide a Pareto front or convergence to yield the optimal solution [55]. However, the comparative analysis between HOMER and other heuristic tech­ niques such as GA, PSO reveal that the outcome of the cost function is comparable [51,52]. Although it is impossible to determine the quality of the solution of the HOMER, a comparative analysis between HOMER and other intelligent techniques (e.g., PSO, GA etc) can give a fair idea about the quality of the HOMER solution. Therefore, the present study is further extended to compare the outcome of HOMER with the GA optimisation technique. Therefore, to justify the quality of solution, the present study also compares the outcome of this study with the GA optimization technique.

5) and introduced in the HOMER optimisation tool along with the technical characteristics and economic data of different components (Table 4).
In the second phase, an investigation delivers a group of hybrid system options showing the minimisation of NPC and COE under specified constraints.
In the third phase, the different system configurations are compared in terms of their technical, economic, and environmental parameters in order to select the optimal hybrid option.
In summary, the simulation uses energy balance of HES components with the given constraints, load profile, and meteorological data to calculate the costs.
HOMER then displays a list of configurations, sorted by net present cost.
In this process, the best solution is selected from among all scenarios depending on the selected criterion (e.g. minimi­ zation of net present costs).
In this process, HOMER does not provide a Pareto front or convergence to yield the optimal solution [55].
However, the comparative analysis between HOMER and other heuristic tech­ niques such as GA, PSO reveal that the outcome of the cost function is comparable [51,52].

Although it is impossible to determine the quality of the solution of the HOMER, a comparative analysis between HOMER and other intelligent techniques (e.g., PSO, GA etc) can give a fair idea about the quality of the HOMER solution.
Therefore, the present study is further extended to compare the outcome of HOMER with the GA optimisation technique.
Therefore, to justify the quality of solution, the present study also compares the outcome of this study with the GA optimization technique.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The GA optimization technique is used for sizing the PV/Diesel/PHSbased HES for minimizing the NPC $(\$)$ under a certain reliability (LPSP $=0\%$ ). The objective function and the constraints are established in a MATLAB M-file based on the load following dispatch strategy and the energy balance of HES components. The HES components data related to technical, economic, and environmental details are incorporated into the objective function and constraints. The GA optimization parameters are population size (300), selection, crossover rate, mutation rate, and maximum generation (1000) selected as stopping criteria. The LPSP is calculated for each population, and the population, which cannot satisfy the predefined LPSP, is discarded from the next generation to continue the process until the maximum generation is reached. The detailed of the GA can be found in the literature [77,78]. The convergence of the GA optimisation process is shown in Fig. 6.

The detailed analysis and results are discussed in the following sections.

Furthermore, the economic benefits related to the payback period for the diesel/PHS system and the effects of the scal­ ability of the diesel generator and load demand are analysed.
The detailed analysis and results are discussed in the following sections.

In summary, the proposed PV/ Diesel/PHS option appears to be a more financially attractive and profitable venture than the PV/PHS and Diesel/PHS systems. unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The environmental emissions from the PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro sys­ tem are substantially lower than those from the Diesel/Pump-hydrobased hybrid one. It is noticeable in Table 8 that the former generates fewer $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions $(47,158~\mathrm{kg/yr})$ than the latter $(224,858~\mathrm{kg/yr})$ , whereas, the PV/Pump-hydro system produces no operational emis­ sions. An alternative explanation of this situation is that the higher RFs of the PV/Pump-hydro $(100\%)$ and PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro $(84\%)$ sys­ tems than the Diesel/Pump-hydro $(0\%)$ one can be attributed to their lower environmental emissions. The more interesting results from this analysis are that the PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro-based hybrid system pro­ duces lower environmental emissions than the PV/Diesel/Battery one. For example, in Table 8, it appears that the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions generated by the former are $47,158\mathrm{kg/yr}$ , while this value for the latter is $64,934\mathrm{kg/}$ yr. From Table 8, it is also evident that the CO, UHC, PM, $S O_{2},$ and $\mathrm{NO}_{\mathrm{x}}$ emissions are lower in PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro option than these of the PV/Diesel/Battery and Diesel/pump-hydro ones. For example, the $\mathrm{NO}_{\mathbf{X}}$ emission for the hybrid PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro, Diesel/pump-hydro, and PV/Diesel/Battery options are $76.1\mathrm{kg/yr}$ , $363\mathrm{kg/yr}$ , and $105~\mathrm{kg/}$ yr, respectively. Similar trends are also true for other emissions. Therefore, the implementation of the proposed hybrid option illustrates a substantial reduction of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions than the diesel-only and hybrid one with battery storage systems.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: In this section, the systems’ environmental emissions are compared in terms of their operational $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions. In Fig. 15, it is apparent that the optimised hybrid system (PV/Diesel/PHS) generates the lowest amount of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ . It is worth noting that the battery-based hybrid system produces $30\%$ higher operational $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions than the pump-based one when a similar load demand is satisfied. Using a factor of 0.465 $\mathrm{CO_{2}k g/k W h}$ for Bangladesh’s grid electricity [79], the total generation of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ required to meet a 205,130 kWh load demand is $95,385\mathrm{kg/yr}$ . It is clearly seen that the proposed PHS-based HES is environmentally sustainable compared to the grid electricity. In comparison with kero­ sene, which generates $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ of $61{,}594~\mathrm{kg/yr}$ , the proposed HES (47,158 $\mathrm{kg/yr)}$ is environmentally benefitted. Additionally, the Diesel/PHS produces the highest operational $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions $(224,858~\mathrm{kg/yr}).$ Therefore, the proposed PV/Diesel/PHS option is clearly beneficial in terms of environmental aspect over the other studied options.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The outcomes optimised by the HOMER software of the proposed PV/Diesel/PHS-based HES are compared with the GA optimisation technique, as reported in Table 9. Results reveal that the NPC $(\$501,399)$ and COE $(0.226\Phi/\mathrm{kWh})$ for the proposed HES is lower while sized by the GA optimisation technique than the HOMER software $(\mathrm{NPC}{=}\$524,791$ and $\mathrm{COE}=0.24\Phi/\mathrm{kWh})$ . This is because the GA option selects 50 kW diesel generator, which results in lower fuel cost compared to HOMER despite having higher PV capacity in the former technique than the latter. The RF $(91\%)$ is higher in GA technique due to the higher PV contribution (272,690kWh/yr) than the HOMER $\left(\mathrm{RF}=\right.$ $80\%$ ). In addition, $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emission of the GA-based sizing offers signifi­ cantly lower than the HOMER one. In summary, the GA-based optimisation technique not only provides cost effective solution but also offers environmentally sustainable sizing option.

source_spans.text: The outcomes optimised by the HOMER software of the proposed PV/Diesel/PHS-based HES are compared with the GA optimisation technique, as reported in Table 9.

This is because the GA option selects 50 kW diesel generator, which results in lower fuel cost compared to HOMER despite having higher PV capacity in the former technique than the latter.
The RF $(91\%)$ is higher in GA technique due to the higher PV contribution (272,690kWh/yr) than the HOMER $\left(\mathrm{RF}=\right.$ $80\%$ ).
In addition, $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emission of the GA-based sizing offers signifi­ cantly lower than the HOMER one.
In summary, the GA-based optimisation technique not only provides cost effective solution but also offers environmentally sustainable sizing option.

In addition, the utilisation of excess energy of HES and heat recovery of diesel engine for meeting thermal demands can be implemented. unchanged_frozen_unit.section: A B S T R A C T
unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: This paper describes a comprehensive analysis of a hybrid energy system (HES) when satisfying the load demand of an off-grid, rural and hilly community in Bangladesh. Different combinations of HES, such as PV/Pump-hydro storage (PHS), Diesel/PHS, and PV/Diesel/Battery, are formulated, analysed, and compared using hybrid opti­ mization of multiple energy resources (HOMER) software. The system configurations, together with the size and selection of system components, are suitably modelled and optimised with the least cost of energy (COE), net present cost (NPC), and $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions. In addition, to illustrate the adaptability and the economic benefits of the studied systems, the scalability of the system is evaluated by changing the load demand and the size of the generator. The study is further extended to include a sensitivity analysis on the uncertain parameters in connection with the climatic data and hardware components. Results indicate that the cost of energy for a pumped HES with a single diesel generator is higher $(0.27\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ than that with two small generators (0.24 $\$/\mathrm{kWh}$ . The energy cost for the optimised PV/Diesel/PHS system $(0.27\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ is found to be significantly lower than those of both PV/PHS (0.43\$/kWh) and Diesel/PHS $(0.41\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ options. This research identifies that the PV/Diesel/PHS system is more cost-effective than the PV/Diesel/Battery-based hybrid system, with cost of en­ ergy at $0.34\$/k W h$ . Results indicate that the genetic algorithm (GA) method provides cost effective and sus­ tainable solution than the HOMER software tool.

These national and international energy exi­ gencies have prompted a search for optimal and renewable energy (RE) solutions to satisfy the increased load requirements in Bangladesh [6]. Although the development of Bangladesh’s power sector in recent years has been remarkable (covering $90\%$ with the grid electricity), its per capita electricity consumption is still significantly lower (382kWh/ capita) than the world’s average (3127 kWh/capita) as well as those of South Asian countries [7]. In addition, the effective implementation and configuration of the RE technologies is still far way off the commercial dimension in Bangladesh [8]. Since the country’s economy is in transi­ tion from the low-level to middle-level income and since the energy consumption and economic development is closely interrelated, the current pace of electricity production is inadequate to satisfy its rising demand [1]. Moreover, the significant share of electricity generated by either natural gas or imported furnace oil or coal contributes to the environmental damage. In this context, environmental emissions can be significantly decreased by reducing the dependency on the conventional fuels and applying innovative RE technologies [9–11]. However, RE resources alone in off-grid areas are currently incapable of providing uninterrupted energy supply due to their unpredictable availability and heavy reliance on the environmental conditions [12–14]. Thus, HESs have been the research focus in recent years. For example, integrating the combustion-based engines or large banks of batteries with the solar PV-based RE systems have already been reported to be financially attractive [6,15,16]. While a short literature review in relation to this research is presented in Section 2 of this paper, it is apparent that the PV/Diesel/PHS-based hybrid system for the mountainous areas in Bangladesh has not been investigated or studied yet. Thus, the key ob­ jectives of this paper include:

These national and international energy exi­ gencies have prompted a search for optimal and renewable energy (RE) solutions to satisfy the increased load requirements in Bangladesh [6]. Although the development of Bangladesh’s power sector in recent years has been remarkable (covering $90\%$ with the grid electricity), its per capita electricity consumption is still significantly lower (382kWh/ capita) than the world’s average (3127 kWh/capita) as well as those of South Asian countries [7]. In addition, the effective implementation and configuration of the RE technologies is still far way off the commercial dimension in Bangladesh [8]. Since the country’s economy is in transi­ tion from the low-level to middle-level income and since the energy consumption and economic development is closely interrelated, the current pace of electricity production is inadequate to satisfy its rising demand [1]. Moreover, the significant share of electricity generated by either natural gas or imported furnace oil or coal contributes to the environmental damage. In this context, environmental emissions can be significantly decreased by reducing the dependency on the conventional fuels and applying innovative RE technologies [9–11]. However, RE resources alone in off-grid areas are currently incapable of providing uninterrupted energy supply due to their unpredictable availability and heavy reliance on the environmental conditions [12–14]. Thus, HESs have been the research focus in recent years. For example, integrating the combustion-based engines or large banks of batteries with the solar PV-based RE systems have already been reported to be financially attractive [6,15,16]. unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Because of the availability, easy installation, high energy and power density, and high efficiency, the electrochemical storage systems are extensively used in the stand-alone HESs, as presented in Table 1. However, their limited lifetimes and the requirement of frequent maintenance are problematic, particularly for areas where access to the mainland is difficult [17,18]. In addition, the disposal of the chemical storage systems poses a practical difficulty in the mountainous areas. Therefore, the mechanical storage systems, such as a pump-hydro op­ tion, could be an alternative to the battery storage systems in the remote areas if a water supply is available. The use of pump-hydro storage in stand-alone power generation facility has recently been emerged to improve the overall sustainability of the low-carbon energy system [19–22]. Its key benefits include a shorter payback period, faster response to the load demand, longer lifetime, and lower maintenance cost than the other systems [23,24].

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: While methods vary from study to study, most of the analyses pre­ sented in Table 2 are clean-energy-based HESs. The study of sizing optimisation is paramount before installing a HES, and it plays a sig­ nificant role in making capital investment decision. In this regard, Kanzumba Kusakana [39] carried out a feasibility study on an off-grid hydrokinetic system configuration with pump-hydro storage for the application in a remote area and found that it was more economic (COE $=0.248\Phi/\mathrm{kWh})$ than a comparable battery storage option $(\mathrm{COE}=0.291\$ $\$1\mathrm{kWh}$ for providing a reliable power supply to the households in the selected zone. However, the author did not examine the load scalability and the uncertainties associated with the meteorological data. Ma et al. [18] optimised a PV/PHS-based power generation scheme for a remote and stand-alone community using a genetic algorithm (GA) and reported that it was economically feasible $\displaystyle{(\mathrm{COE}=0.289\S/\mathrm{kWh})}$ for reliably satisfying the electricity demand. In another study, Ma et al. [40] determined that a PV/Wind/PHS system has more economic benefits than a PV/Wind/Battery system. Unlike these studies, the present study investigates the integration of supplementary prime movers, uncertainty associated with the meteorological data, and the degradation of the hardware systems (PV, and converter). Rathore and Patidar [19] ana­ lysed a PV/Wind/PHS-based stand-alone microgrid system for an offgrid community and reported that a PHS-based system was both economically and environmentally better than a battery-based storage configuration. Another PV/PHS system was examined using a GA with various PV tracking technologies by Shabani and Mahmoudimehr [24] and the results were compared with those for a PV/Battery option. The findings from their study indicated that the latter had a $76\%$ higher COE than the former. Ayodele et al. [41] optimally selected a PHS-based PV/ Wind energy system for a stand-alone community using a binary sortand-search algorithm. They found that a PV/Wind/PHS system had the lowest COE out of all the different configurations studied. A gridintegrated PV/PHS system was studied by Li et al. [42] and they showed that variable renewable energy had significant effects on the balance of a grid’s supply and demand. They investigated this aspect by absorbing the surplus PV power by pump-hydro storage system, which greatly reduced the power output from the studied medium-scale power generation units. It is evident from these analyses that the hybrid sys­ tems supplemented by the diesel generators were not adequately studied and the detailed sensitivity analysis of such systems is scarce in the literature.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: A few studies have been reported on the PV/Diesel/PHS system. In this context, Awan et al. unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Eltamaly et al. [50] carried out a load management strategy to determine the optimal size of the PV/Wind/Diesel/FC/Battery-based HES using PSO technique and compared with the HOMER. They considered two different types of load demand on priority basis such as high and low. They found that the COE was comparable between PSO algorithm (0.2805\$/kWh) and HOMER (0.2774\$/kWh) when both loads were considered. However, they varied only the low priority load demand and did not consider the scalability of load demand i.e. increasing or decreasing the total load requirements. A hybrid PV/ Wind/Battery was optimised using GA-PSO by Ghorbani et al. [51] and compared with the HOMER. The authors reported that the GA-PSO had slightly lower, yet comparable COE (0.508\$/kWh) than that of the HOMER $(0.51\$14)$ . In another study, Fodhil et al. [52] also found that the PSO offers lower cost (0.38\$/kWh) than the HOMER (0.40 $\$1\mathrm{kWh}$ in optimising the HES. In this study, HOMER tool is used because of its simplicity [53] and quick searching ability [54] to find the optimal sizing of the hardware components. Although the current study uses the standard HOMER tool, the analysis goes beyond the standard application of HOMER by thoroughly examining the objective functions, the various uncertainties, and the different consequential performance indicators.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: A schematic layout of the PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro storage system designed to satisfy the load demand $(\mathrm{P_{L}})$ of a small remote community consisting of 50 households is presented in Fig. 1. A direct current (DC) load bus is linked to the PV panel while the alternative current (AC) bus is connected with both diesel generator and the pump-hydro storage system. The DC power generated by the PV module $(\mathrm{P_{PV}})$ is converted to AC power $(\mathrm{{P}_{\mathrm{{inv}}}})$ through an inverter. The excess energy (EE) produced by the PV module after the load demand is satisfied is used to power the pump $(\mathrm{P_{P}})$ to either lift water $\left(\mathsf{Q}_{\mathsf{w}}\right)$ to the upper reservoir or drain down to the lower basin $(\mathrm{\bfP_{EE}})$ when the reservoir reaches its maximum level. The turbine is used to supply power $(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{T}})$ when the production of PV power is not sufficient to meet the electricity demand and the load is under the specified load ratio of the diesel generator ( $30\%$ of its rated power).

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: A well-structured framework is necessary to optimise a HES that can consistently satisfy the load requirements for a stand-alone remote area. The optimisation framework representing this current study is shown in Fig. 2. The HOMER software operates in three different phases. In the first phase, a conceptual system architecture (Fig. 1) is developed based on existing renewable energy and meteorological data. In this phase, the electric power requirement of the selected site is also assessed (Table 3 and presented in Fig. 5) and introduced in the HOMER optimisation tool along with the technical characteristics and economic data of different components (Table 4). In the second phase, an investigation delivers a group of hybrid system options showing the minimisation of NPC and COE under specified constraints. In the third phase, the different system configurations are compared in terms of their technical, economic, and environmental parameters in order to select the optimal hybrid option. In summary, the simulation uses energy balance of HES components with the given constraints, load profile, and meteorological data to calculate the costs. HOMER then displays a list of configurations, sorted by net present cost. In this process, the best solution is selected from among all scenarios depending on the selected criterion (e.g. minimi­ zation of net present costs). In this process, HOMER does not provide a Pareto front or convergence to yield the optimal solution [55]. However, the comparative analysis between HOMER and other heuristic tech­ niques such as GA, PSO reveal that the outcome of the cost function is comparable [51,52]. Although it is impossible to determine the quality of the solution of the HOMER, a comparative analysis between HOMER and other intelligent techniques (e.g., PSO, GA etc) can give a fair idea about the quality of the HOMER solution. Therefore, the present study is further extended to compare the outcome of HOMER with the GA optimisation technique. Therefore, to justify the quality of solution, the present study also compares the outcome of this study with the GA optimization technique.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: A well-structured framework is necessary to optimise a HES that can consistently satisfy the load requirements for a stand-alone remote area. The optimisation framework representing this current study is shown in Fig. 2. The HOMER software operates in three different phases. In the first phase, a conceptual system architecture (Fig. 1) is developed based on existing renewable energy and meteorological data. In this phase, the electric power requirement of the selected site is also assessed (Table 3 and presented in Fig. 5) and introduced in the HOMER optimisation tool along with the technical characteristics and economic data of different components (Table 4). In the second phase, an investigation delivers a group of hybrid system options showing the minimisation of NPC and COE under specified constraints. In the third phase, the different system configurations are compared in terms of their technical, economic, and environmental parameters in order to select the optimal hybrid option. In summary, the simulation uses energy balance of HES components with the given constraints, load profile, and meteorological data to calculate the costs. HOMER then displays a list of configurations, sorted by net present cost. In this process, the best solution is selected from among all scenarios depending on the selected criterion (e.g. minimi­ zation of net present costs). In this process, HOMER does not provide a Pareto front or convergence to yield the optimal solution [55]. However, the comparative analysis between HOMER and other heuristic tech­ niques such as GA, PSO reveal that the outcome of the cost function is comparable [51,52]. Although it is impossible to determine the quality of the solution of the HOMER, a comparative analysis between HOMER and other intelligent techniques (e.g., PSO, GA etc) can give a fair idea about the quality of the HOMER solution. Therefore, the present study is further extended to compare the outcome of HOMER with the GA optimisation technique. Therefore, to justify the quality of solution, the present study also compares the outcome of this study with the GA optimization technique.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The GA optimization technique is used for sizing the PV/Diesel/PHSbased HES for minimizing the NPC $(\$)$ under a certain reliability (LPSP $=0\%$ ). The objective function and the constraints are established in a MATLAB M-file based on the load following dispatch strategy and the energy balance of HES components. The HES components data related to technical, economic, and environmental details are incorporated into the objective function and constraints. The GA optimization parameters are population size (300), selection, crossover rate, mutation rate, and maximum generation (1000) selected as stopping criteria. The LPSP is calculated for each population, and the population, which cannot satisfy the predefined LPSP, is discarded from the next generation to continue the process until the maximum generation is reached. The detailed of the GA can be found in the literature [77,78]. The convergence of the GA optimisation process is shown in Fig. 6.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The analysis is extended to compare the PHS and battery storage (lead-acid battery) systems. The COE of the PV/Diesel/PHS system is found to be lower $(0.27\$40$ than that of the PV/Diesel/Batterybased one $(0.34\$/\mathrm{kWh})$ , as can be seen in Table 6. Their NPCs also show similar trends mainly because the latter has higher capital and replacement costs $\$35,004$ and $\$11,020$ , respectively compared with $\$29,916$ and $\$2,003$ , respectively), as shown in Table 7. Although Diesel/PHS requires lower capital investment, the system needs continuous monetary injection for purchasing fuel (refer resource cost), which makes the annualised cost (\$84,849) to be higher than the PV/ Diesel/PHS $(\$55,005)$ one. On the other hand, PV/Battery system scores the highest capital investment (\$102,908) among all the systems re­ ported in Table 7. Halabi et al. [60] conducted a performance analysis of a PV/Diesel/Battery system using the HOMER and found that its COE was $0.31\$40$ for Malaysian conditions which is comparable with that of the battery-based hybrid option in this study. The COE found in the present study is slightly lower than that of the authors’ previous study $(0.37\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ , which considered a PV/Diesel/Battery system [8]. It can also be seen in Table 6 that the battery-based system requires a larger capacity battery storage (884kWh) than the pump-storage one (762kWh). The RF of the PV/Diesel/PHS system is higher $(84\%)$ than that of the PV/Diesel/Battery option $(76\%)$ , which is attributable to the lower contribution made by the diesel generator (39,205kWh/yr) in the former than that by the latter (54,002kWh/yr), as presented in Table 6. However, the DF (73kWh/start-stop/yr) is slightly lower for the PV/ Diesel/Pump-hydro system than that for the PV/Diesel/Battery (77kWh/start-stop/yr) one. On the other hand, the COE is $146\%$ higher for the latter than the former, because it requires a larger-capacity PV module due mainly to its battery charging/discharging functions when meeting a similar load demand. Therefore, the implementation of a PV/ Diesel/PHS option is not only more financially viable choice but also technically attractive compared with the PV/Diesel/Battery system.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: This research also examines the effects of a single large-capacity diesel generator $(100~\mathrm{kW})$ versus two smaller ones $(2\times50~\mathrm{kW})$ in terms of the cost and system performance. It is obvious from the results presented in Table 6 that the unit cost of energy of the PV/PHS system with 2 smaller generator sets is slightly lower $(0.24~\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ than that with the larger single-capacity diesel generator set $(0.27\$1)$ ). This is because the latter has a higher minimum load ratio of $30\mathrm{kW}$ ( $30\%$ of the rated capacity for $100~\mathrm{kW})$ ) required to start the generator than that of the former of $15~\mathrm{kW}$ ( $30\%$ of the rated capacity for $50~\mathrm{kW}$ ). Therefore, the energy generated by the PV module is higher in the latter (243,509kWh/yr) than the former (212,244kWh/yr), as revealed in Table 6. Alternatively, the energy generation from a large generator is lower (39,205kWh/yr) than that of the two smaller generators (53,755kWh/yr). In this context, the system requires a higher capacity of the PV module (156 kW) to satisfy the load demand which is under the minimum load ratio for the larger-capacity engine. In addition, the RF for the former option is slightly higher $(84\%)$ than that of the later $(80\%)$ one, and consequently, the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions in the former are lower than the later. In summary, the hybrid PV/Pump-hydro with two smaller diesel generators has COE at the cost of RF and $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The environmental emissions from the PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro sys­ tem are substantially lower than those from the Diesel/Pump-hydrobased hybrid one. It is noticeable in Table 8 that the former generates fewer $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions $(47,158~\mathrm{kg/yr})$ than the latter $(224,858~\mathrm{kg/yr})$ , whereas, the PV/Pump-hydro system produces no operational emis­ sions. An alternative explanation of this situation is that the higher RFs of the PV/Pump-hydro $(100\%)$ and PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro $(84\%)$ sys­ tems than the Diesel/Pump-hydro $(0\%)$ one can be attributed to their lower environmental emissions. The more interesting results from this analysis are that the PV/Diesel/Pump-hydro-based hybrid system pro­ duces lower environmental emissions than the PV/Diesel/Battery one. For example, in Table 8, it appears that the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions generated by the former are $47,158\mathrm{kg/yr}$ , while this value for the latter is $64,934\mathrm{kg/}$ yr. Additionally, the Diesel/PHS produces the highest operational $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions $(224,858~\mathrm{kg/yr}).$ Therefore, the proposed PV/Diesel/PHS option is clearly beneficial in terms of environmental aspect over the other studied options.

source_spans.text: In this study, a PV/Diesel/PHS-based HES is analysed and optimised, which meets the load demand of a remote community in Bangladesh.
The optimisation framework assesses different configurations, such as PV/PHS, Diesel/PHS, and PV/Diesel/Battery systems, in terms of their costs, emissions, and performance indicators.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: The analysis is extended to compare the PHS and battery storage (lead-acid battery) systems. The COE of the PV/Diesel/PHS system is found to be lower $(0.27\$40$ than that of the PV/Diesel/Batterybased one $(0.34\$/\mathrm{kWh})$ , as can be seen in Table 6. Their NPCs also show similar trends mainly because the latter has higher capital and replacement costs $\$35,004$ and $\$11,020$ , respectively compared with $\$29,916$ and $\$2,003$ , respectively), as shown in Table 7. Although Diesel/PHS requires lower capital investment, the system needs continuous monetary injection for purchasing fuel (refer resource cost), which makes the annualised cost (\$84,849) to be higher than the PV/ Diesel/PHS $(\$55,005)$ one. On the other hand, PV/Battery system scores the highest capital investment (\$102,908) among all the systems re­ ported in Table 7. Halabi et al. [60] conducted a performance analysis of a PV/Diesel/Battery system using the HOMER and found that its COE was $0.31\$40$ for Malaysian conditions which is comparable with that of the battery-based hybrid option in this study. The COE found in the present study is slightly lower than that of the authors’ previous study $(0.37\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ , which considered a PV/Diesel/Battery system [8]. It can also be seen in Table 6 that the battery-based system requires a larger capacity battery storage (884kWh) than the pump-storage one (762kWh). The RF of the PV/Diesel/PHS system is higher $(84\%)$ than that of the PV/Diesel/Battery option $(76\%)$ , which is attributable to the lower contribution made by the diesel generator (39,205kWh/yr) in the former than that by the latter (54,002kWh/yr), as presented in Table 6. However, the DF (73kWh/start-stop/yr) is slightly lower for the PV/ Diesel/Pump-hydro system than that for the PV/Diesel/Battery (77kWh/start-stop/yr) one. On the other hand, the COE is $146\%$ higher for the latter than the former, because it requires a larger-capacity PV module due mainly to its battery charging/discharging functions when meeting a similar load demand. Therefore, the implementation of a PV/ Diesel/PHS option is not only more financially viable choice but also technically attractive compared with the PV/Diesel/Battery system.

source_spans.text: The analysis is extended to compare the PHS and battery storage (lead-acid battery) systems.
The COE of the PV/Diesel/PHS system is found to be lower $(0.27\$40$ than that of the PV/Diesel/Batterybased one $(0.34\$/\mathrm{kWh})$ , as can be seen in Table 6.

Their NPCs also show similar trends mainly because the latter has higher capital and replacement costs $\$35,004$ and $\$11,020$ , respectively compared with $\$29,916$ and $\$2,003$ , respectively), as shown in Table 7.

Although Diesel/PHS requires lower capital investment, the system needs continuous monetary injection for purchasing fuel (refer resource cost), which makes the annualised cost (\$84,849) to be higher than the PV/ Diesel/PHS $(\$55,005)$ one.
On the other hand, PV/Battery system scores the highest capital investment (\$102,908) among all the systems re­ ported in Table 7.

Halabi et al. [60] conducted a performance analysis of a PV/Diesel/Battery system using the HOMER and found that its COE was $0.31\$40$ for Malaysian conditions which is comparable with that of the battery-based hybrid option in this study.
The COE found in the present study is slightly lower than that of the authors’ previous study $(0.37\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ , which considered a PV/Diesel/Battery system [8].
It can also be seen in Table 6 that the battery-based system requires a larger capacity battery storage (884kWh) than the pump-storage one (762kWh).

The RF of the PV/Diesel/PHS system is higher $(84\%)$ than that of the PV/Diesel/Battery option $(76\%)$ , which is attributable to the lower contribution made by the diesel generator (39,205kWh/yr) in the former than that by the latter (54,002kWh/yr), as presented in Table 6.
However, the DF (73kWh/start-stop/yr) is slightly lower for the PV/ Diesel/Pump-hydro system than that for the PV/Diesel/Battery (77kWh/start-stop/yr) one.

On the other hand, the COE is $146\%$ higher for the latter than the former, because it requires a larger-capacity PV module due mainly to its battery charging/discharging functions when meeting a similar load demand.
Therefore, the implementation of a PV/ Diesel/PHS option is not only more financially viable choice but also technically attractive compared with the PV/Diesel/Battery system.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: This research also examines the effects of a single large-capacity diesel generator $(100~\mathrm{kW})$ versus two smaller ones $(2\times50~\mathrm{kW})$ in terms of the cost and system performance. It is obvious from the results presented in Table 6 that the unit cost of energy of the PV/PHS system with 2 smaller generator sets is slightly lower $(0.24~\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ than that with the larger single-capacity diesel generator set $(0.27\$1)$ ). This is because the latter has a higher minimum load ratio of $30\mathrm{kW}$ ( $30\%$ of the rated capacity for $100~\mathrm{kW})$ ) required to start the generator than that of the former of $15~\mathrm{kW}$ ( $30\%$ of the rated capacity for $50~\mathrm{kW}$ ). Therefore, the energy generated by the PV module is higher in the latter (243,509kWh/yr) than the former (212,244kWh/yr), as revealed in Table 6. Alternatively, the energy generation from a large generator is lower (39,205kWh/yr) than that of the two smaller generators (53,755kWh/yr). In this context, the system requires a higher capacity of the PV module (156 kW) to satisfy the load demand which is under the minimum load ratio for the larger-capacity engine. In addition, the RF for the former option is slightly higher $(84\%)$ than that of the later $(80\%)$ one, and consequently, the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions in the former are lower than the later. In summary, the hybrid PV/Pump-hydro with two smaller diesel generators has COE at the cost of RF and $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions.

It is obvious from the results presented in Table 6 that the unit cost of energy of the PV/PHS system with 2 smaller generator sets is slightly lower $(0.24~\S/\mathrm{kWh})$ than that with the larger single-capacity diesel generator set $(0.27\$1)$ ).

This is because the latter has a higher minimum load ratio of $30\mathrm{kW}$ ( $30\%$ of the rated capacity for $100~\mathrm{kW})$ ) required to start the generator than that of the former of $15~\mathrm{kW}$ ( $30\%$ of the rated capacity for $50~\mathrm{kW}$ ).
Therefore, the energy generated by the PV module is higher in the latter (243,509kWh/yr) than the former (212,244kWh/yr), as revealed in Table 6.
Alternatively, the energy generation from a large generator is lower (39,205kWh/yr) than that of the two smaller generators (53,755kWh/yr).
In this context, the system requires a higher capacity of the PV module (156 kW) to satisfy the load demand which is under the minimum load ratio for the larger-capacity engine.
In addition, the RF for the former option is slightly higher $(84\%)$ than that of the later $(80\%)$ one, and consequently, the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions in the former are lower than the later.
In summary, the hybrid PV/Pump-hydro with two smaller diesel generators has COE at the cost of RF and $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ emissions.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: In the above analysis, the load demand is considered to be 205,130 kWh/yr which covers a community of 50 households. Then, considering a community with a different number of households, a techno-economic analysis is conducted to study the effects of a load’s scalability on the COE and the NPC (Fig. 13), and the RF and the EE (Fig. 14). The out­ comes indicate that the COE decreases slightly when the load demand (number of households) increases. This occurs because, at any instant, it can be met by the minimum load ratio of the diesel generator. When the number of households increases from 50 to 70, the COE decreases from $0.27\$100$ to $0.26\$4$ , whereas the NPC rises from $\$595,123$ to $\$797,628$ .
